questions.q: Which is true for an element $X$~present in the~${13}^{th}$& group of the periodic table?
options: It is a gas at room temperature.
It forms an oxide of formula ${X}_{2}{O}_{3}$.
It forms a chloride of formula ${XCl}_{2}$.
questions.solution:
The elements of group$- 13$ of the periodic table are solids (examples: $B, Al$, etc.) at room temperature.

They have a common oxidation state of $+ 3$ (as they have three valence electrons in the outermost shell).
So, they form an oxide of formula ${X}_{2}{O}_{3}$ from the ions $X^{3 +}$ and $O^{2 -}$.~

It forms a metal chloride of formula ${XCl}_{3}$~and dimer ${X}_{2}{Cl}_{6}$& as the octet state, which accounts for stability& is not fulfilled for the metal in the monomer.

questions.q: $Ge$ (II) compounds are powerful reducing agents whereas $Pb$ (IV) compounds are strong oxidants. It is due to -

Ionic radii of ${Pb}^{2 +}$ and ${Pb}^{4 +}$ are larger than those of ${Ge}^{2 +}$ and ${Ge}^{4 +}$
More pronounced inert pair effect in lead than in $Ge$
questions.solution: Due to inert pair effect, the $+ 2$ oxidation state stability increases down the${14}^{th}$ group, and $+ 4$ oxidation state stability decreases down the group. $Ge ( II )$ tends to acquire $Ge ( IV )$ state by loss of electrons. questions.q: Which one of the following methods is used to prepare carbon monoxide on commercial scale?
options: Dehydration of formic acid with conc. $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$
Direct oxidation of C in limited supply of oxygen
questions.solution: (a) When formic acid $\mathrm{HCOOH}$ is dehydrated with $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ (conc.), it gives carbon monoxide (CO) and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ as : \mathrm{HCOOH}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 \text { (conc.) } \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 But the above process is not used on commercial scale. (b) Direct oxidation of carbon in limited supply of oxygen can give $\mathrm{CO}$ but the process is not used on commercial scale. 2 \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{O}_2 \text { (limited supply) } \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO} (c) When steam  \left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)$ is passed over coke $(\mathrm{C})$, it gives $\mathrm{CO}+\mathrm{H}_2$, as : \text { Coke }(\mathrm{C})+\underset{(\text { Steam) }}{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}} \stackrel{\Delta}{\mathrm{Ni}} \mathrm{CO}(g)+\mathrm{H}_2(g) The above process can be used to produce (CO) on commercial scale. (d) Lime stone is $\mathrm{CaCO}_3$, on heating it gives oxygen  \left(\mathrm{O}_2\right)$ and $\mathrm{CaO}$ as : \mathrm{CaCO}_3 \stackrel{\Delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{O}_2 Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.solution: (I) Catenation property of group 14 elements decreases from carbon to tin. Carbon is small atom, thus the bond formed between two carbon atom is strong. Thus, lead does not show catenation property. (II) Fullerene  \left(\mathrm{C}_{60}\right)$ has 20 six-membered carbon rings and 12 five-membered carbon rings. (III) $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ is soluble in $\mathrm{NaOH}$ or alkaline solution. $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ is an acidic oxide. 2 $\mathrm{NaOH}+\mathrm{SiO}}_{2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}}_{2} $\mathrm{SiO}}_{3}+ \mathrm{H}}_{2} $\mathrm{O}$Thus, option (2) is correct.$

$\begin{cases}\text{Ca} {\left({HCO}_{3}\right)}_{2} & \overset{Heat}{⟶} & {CaCO}_{3} & + & {CO}_{2} & + & {H}_{2} \text{O} \\ & & & & \left(\text{B}\right) & & \end{cases}$

A and B are $C{O}_{2}$ and $C{O}_{2}$ .
